# Determinants of Using AI-Based Chatbots for Knowledge Sharing: Evidence From PLS-SEM and Fuzzy Sets (fsQCA)
Mostafa Al-Emran<sup>®</sup>, Adi Ahmad AlQudah<sup>®</sup>, Ghazanfar Ali Abbasi<sup>®</sup>, Mohammed A. Al-Sharafi<sup>®</sup>, and Mohammad Iranmanesh<sup>®</sup>
Abstract—While adopting chatbots powered by artificial intelligence could enhance knowledge sharing, it also causes challenges due to the "dark side" of these agents. However, research on the factors influencing chatbots for knowledge sharing is lacking. To bridge this gap, we developed the integrated chatbot acceptanceavoidance model, which looks at the positive and negative determinants of using chatbots for knowledge sharing. Through a comprehensive questionnaire survey of 447 students, the research model is evaluated using the partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), a symmetric approach, and fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) as an asymmetric approach. The PLS-SEM results supported the positive role of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and habit and the negative role of perceived threats in affecting chatbot use for knowledge sharing. Although PLS-SEM results revealed that social influence, facilitating conditions, and hedonic motivation have no impact on chatbot use, the fsQCA analysis revealed that all factors might play a role in shaping the use of chatbots. In addition to the theoretical contributions, the findings provide several managerial implications for universities, instructors, and chatbot developers to help them make insightful decisions and promote the use of chatbots.

# I. Introduction
ITH the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, including machine learning and deep learning, chatbots or conversational agents mainly relying on natural language processing have grown considerably. Chatbots are computerized programs that chat and interact with humans to perform specific tasks using a natural language [1]. The birth of robotics in 1921 laid the foundations for today's chatbot industry [2]. The idea of chatbots gained further traction with the release of Apple's Siri, which mainly relies on chatbot technologies. AI algorithms allow chatbots to identify information accurately and learn from their data by predicting results. AI-powered chatbots are now being further customized to better comprehend human interactions and respond to them in a similar natural language that humans would understand if they were human agents [2].
Users communicate with chatbots to get real-time information about products or services [3]. By 2023, businesses are expected to save 2.5 billion hours due to chatbots [4]. Global chatbot revenues are expected to reach $455 million by 2027 [5]. As a result, chatbots have been used in a variety of industries to deliver tailored product information, handle customer care queries, and assist customers with placing orders [6]. Specifically, in the education domain, chatbots are being used more often because they facilitate timely and customized responses [7]. Chatbots aid in enhancing engagement among students, boosting peer, content, and environmental communication, improving learning performance, and promoting collaborative learning [8]. These conversational agents have also been utilized to support administrative tasks, teaching and learning, research and development, and student evaluation. When it comes to supporting learning activities, chatbots can assist students in addressing various topics and encouraging reflection in response to their initial queries [9].
Among several knowledge management factors, a recent study showed that knowledge sharing contributes to only 19% of students' adoption of chatbots in educational settings [10]. According to the technology threat avoidance theory (TTAT), people's perceptions of their susceptibility to and the severity of technology threats affect their awareness of those threats,

At the same time, understanding what impacts the adoption of chatbots in general [[12]](#page-11-0) and their use for educational purposes [[10]](#page-11-0) still needs more exploration. Furthermore, earlier studies focused on consumers' adoption of chatbots for business services [[13]](#page-11-0) and disregarded their usage for learning activities. The individualistic sociotechnical environments were the main emphasis of earlier studies, with the collectivistic contexts receiving minimal attention [[10].](#page-11-0)
As a result, students' use of chatbots for knowledge sharing is likely to be influenced by both risks and benefits resulting from using these agents. However, there are no models that explain and predict IT adoption by concurrently considering both benefits and concerns [[14].](#page-11-0) While this is addressed in a recent study by integrating unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and TTAT to explain AI adoption for decision-making [[15],](#page-11-0) most of the UTAUT's beneficial factors, such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions, did not support the intention to use AI at the organizational level. To bridge the aforementioned research gaps, our study draws on UTAUT2 and TTAT to develop an integrated chatbot acceptance-avoidance model (ICAAM) to investigate the beneficial and risky factors affecting the use of chatbots for knowledge sharing among university students, contributing to the individual level.
It's worth mentioning that the existing literature solely relies on a symmetrical approach, namely structural equation modeling (SEM), mainly based on net effect modeling. The employment of asymmetrical modeling as the main method in technology adoption and specifically in using chatbots is scarce, and the oversight of causally correlated variables is noteworthy [[16].](#page-11-0) By using fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), mechanisms that symmetrical methods would have missed are uncovered [[17].](#page-11-0) As a result, to provide a better outcome, the fsQCA results will help make more accurate predictions by illuminating the causal models. To investigate and identify the "sufficient" and "necessary" conditions of various determinants that influence individuals' use of chatbots for knowledge sharing, this study uses a hybrid approach that combines symmetrical and asymmetrical analysis through PLS-SEM and fsQCA.
# II. LITERATURE REVIEW
## *A. Chatbots Adoption in Education*
A chatbot is a term that describes a conversational agent that refers to any software application involved in a chat with a human via natural language [[18].](#page-11-0) The acceptance of chatbots and their importance for successful adoption were explored across various contexts. In education, for example, Chatterjee and Bhattacharjee [[19]](#page-11-0) highlighted the role of AI-based chatbots in providing accurate and quick responses for studies inquiries, such as inquiries related to admission purposes. Based on the technology acceptance model, Chen et al. [[20]](#page-11-0) explored the crucial role of chatbots in learning Chinese vocabulary and
conducted the study with 58 students who were divided into two independent groups (one-to-many classroom as a control group and one-to-one tutor sessions as experimental group). The study confirms that chatbots can encourage students' learning curves and achievements in learning the Chinese language. The oneto-one environment showed better results in comparison with the classroom environment. The results also revealed that perceived usefulness has a considerable influence on the behavioral intention of students to use chatbots. By relying on the UTAUT2 model, Almahri et al. [[21]](#page-11-0) employed an empirical approach to study the influential factors that may facilitate or hinder the adoption of chatbots by students in higher education institutions. The empirical analysis results showed that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and habit were crucial factors in significantly predicting the students' behavioral intention to use chatbots.
The use of chatbots as a language learning tool was studied by Huang et al. [[22]](#page-11-0) through a systematic literature review to find out the potential technological, pedagogical, and social affordances that can be enabled by chatbots to learn first, second, and foreign languages. The review mainly focused on the empirical studies that evaluated the use of chatbots in language learning. The key findings showed that timeliness, ease of use, and personalization were the main technological factors in using chatbots for language learning. Timeliness means that students can have real-time interaction with chatbots at any time, and that can satisfy their needs for the self-learning pace [[20].](#page-11-0) The chatbots' ease of use (e.g., interactive interface) has a significant positive influence on students' expected benefits from language learning [[23].](#page-12-0) Ease of use also enables users to reach chatbots easily through web pages or mobile applications and practice speaking with these chatbots by sending text or voice messages [[22].](#page-11-0)
## *B. Chatbots for Knowledge Sharing*
Knowledge transfer and knowledge sharing are sometimes used interchangeably [[24],](#page-12-0) whereas Paulin and Suneson [[25]](#page-12-0) have clearly differentiated the two terms into different concepts. Knowledge transfer is about the distribution of information from one group of people to another, whereas knowledge sharing is related to the process where the information is shared within a specific group. In general, knowledge sharing is vital to improve the learning process and contribute to building the knowledge workforce, especially in the domain of information technology [[26].](#page-12-0) Concerning chatbots, Mleczko [[27]](#page-12-0) described them as virtual assistants that can share customized knowledge to support various repetitive activities and repair tasks. Chatbots are significantly helpful for sharing knowledge, especially regarding day-to-day business practices and corporate training [[28].](#page-12-0)
Chatbots for knowledge sharing were successfully deployed in various domains. For instance, Bodea et al. [[28]](#page-12-0) have studied the role of chatbots and their applications to exchange knowledge of various project management processes, including collaboration, task management, and usability. The study has clarified how chatbots ensure data consistency concerning timesheets and risk prediction. The study also showed how a team could eliminate the long chain of emails and collaborate
appropriately with automatic schedules and timesheet reminders as supported by chatbots. Additionally, Ong et al. [[24]](#page-12-0) have designed a chatbot application within a dynamic web-based knowledge management system platform to share knowledge in agriculture. The developed platform aims to build a network amongst farmers and related professionals to share knowledge and help young farmers who have just started their agriculture business. The results confirmed that knowledge sharing through chatbots would be beneficial in enhancing product quantities and quality levels.
Educational settings are attractive domains to utilize chatbots, where they are seen as virtual assistants for various events, including training and administrative tasks[[28].](#page-12-0) Apart from learning languages [[20],](#page-11-0) [[22],](#page-11-0) chatbots in educational settings can be used to share various types of information among students. For instance, De Nieva et al. [[29]](#page-12-0) discussed how students could use chatbots to eliminate the negative effects of societal stigma by restriction-free sharing for the stressful situations they may experience due to the massive amount of academic workloads. Another example is using chatbots for medical education [[30],](#page-12-0) where chatbots are viewed as virtual patients [[31]](#page-12-0) that help healthcare practitioners to simulate and share various health conditions. This helps to exchange knowledge among students to reinforce learning and help them quickly find the required information. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is a lack of studies on what affects the use of chatbots for knowledge sharing, specifically in educational settings.
# III. RESEARCH MODEL AND HYPOTHESES DEVELOPMENT
To fulfill the objectives of this study, a theoretical model is developed to understand the factors and their influence on students' use of chatbots for knowledge sharing. It is expected that using chatbots for knowledge sharing can face positive and negative influences, but a quick review of the literature indicated that both influences were not explored through proper models to predict the actual use of information technologies [[14],](#page-11-0) [[15].](#page-11-0)
UTAUT was primarily proposed to understand the organizational contexts and their staff [[32],](#page-12-0) with limitations to explore voluntary use [[33].](#page-12-0) Consumers' behaviors are voluntary, so the second-generation (UTAUT2) was specifically proposed by Venkatesh et al. [[34]](#page-12-0) to explain the technology acceptance from the perspective of consumers. UTAUT2 comprises almost all the factors that can explain the actual use of chatbot solutions for knowledge sharing. Therefore, it is selected as a foundation model to propose the theoretical model in this research. On the other hand, although UTAUT2 was extensively utilized to explore the behavioral intention and actual use of information technologies, it does not consider the concerns of users and their negative thoughts. Besides, the acceptance theories for information technologies were not designed to explore avoidance behavior[[35].](#page-12-0) Numerous studies have focused on the importance of discovering the "dark side" of technology use and its related factors of technophobia, technostress, and anxiety [[15],](#page-11-0) [[36].](#page-12-0)
Based on the literature and the particularity of chatbot usage by students to share knowledge, the research model in Fig. [1](#page-3-0) presents ICAAM. ICAAM is inspired and underpinned by Cao
et al. [[15],](#page-11-0) along with the key constructs of the UTAUT2. It is imperative to highlight that ICAAM did not include the behavioral intention construct, as this study focuses on the actual users of chatbots [[37].](#page-12-0) Furthermore, the "price value" construct is related to the price that a consumer will pay to use a specific commodity [[38],](#page-12-0) which is not compatible with the case of this study since the students will not pay for the service. Therefore, the price value factor was dropped from the proposed model because it is not relevant to the current context [[21],](#page-11-0) [[38].](#page-12-0) It is also crucial to report that the moderators (e.g., gender, age, and experience) were eliminated from the proposed ICAAM. The reason behind this elimination is to build a context-generic model that can directly examine the associations between its constructs [[39],](#page-12-0) [[40],](#page-12-0) and the possibility that moderators may not affect technology use across all contexts [[41].](#page-12-0)
## *A. Performance Expectancy*
As defined by Venkatesh et al. [[34],](#page-12-0) performance expectancy is the extent to which a person believes that a specific technology is beneficial to obtain better gains in job performance. People are more motivated to use specific technology if they feel it is more beneficial to complete their tasks [[42].](#page-12-0) Several studies have confirmed that performance expectancy has the most significant influence on accepting and using technologies [[37],](#page-12-0) [[43].](#page-12-0) More specifically, Sugumar and Chandra [[38]](#page-12-0) confirmed that performance expectancy has a significant influence on adopting chatbots for financial services. Alt et al. [[44]](#page-12-0) also found that performance expectancy has a significant effect on customers' intention to use chatbots for banking services. Furthermore, Almahri et al. [[21]](#page-11-0) supported the significant influence of performance expectancy on the intention to accept and use chatbots by students in U.K. universities. Consequently, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H1:* Performance expectancy has a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *B. Effort Expectancy*
Effort expectancy refers to "the degree of ease associated with the use of the system" [[32].](#page-12-0) The user's efforts to use a particular information technology play a significant role in using and accepting that technology [[45],](#page-12-0) [[46].](#page-12-0) In the context of chatbots, Rodríguez Cardona et al.[[45]](#page-12-0) confirmed the significant influence of effort expectancy on the behavioral intention to use and accept chatbots in the insurance business. Similarly, Almahri et al. [[21]](#page-11-0) found that effort expectancy has a significant positive influence on the behavioral intention of students to use chatbots. These observations suggest that students would be interested in using chatbots for knowledge sharing if they found them easy and user-friendly. So, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H2:* Effort expectancy has a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *C. Social Influence*
Social influence refers to "the extent to which an individual perceives that important others believe he or she should apply

Additionally, successful chatbot adoption depends on society and community use rather than being used from an individual or self-perspective. In their study, Kim et al. [[48]](#page-12-0) confirmed the importance of social influence in predicting the acceptance of chatbots for knowledge sharing by people vulnerable to Tuberculosis in South Korea. In line with this, it is argued that the stronger peer groups' influence, the stronger the behavioral intention to use chatbots [[47].](#page-12-0) Consequently, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H3:* Social influence has a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *D. Facilitating Conditions*
Facilitating conditions refer to "the degree to which an individual believes that an organizational and technical infrastructure exists to support the use of the system" [[32].](#page-12-0) The presence of assistance, such as top management, instructions, and manuals for using information technology, is a priority for facilitating conditions [[49].](#page-12-0) In general, the use of technologies needs a specific level of skills and infrastructure (e.g., laptops
and proper Internet connection). So, it is common sense that the availability of a proper setup can encourage students to use chatbots for knowledge sharing. The significant positive influence of facilitating conditions on behavioral intention and actual use of information technologies was verified in many studies across different contexts [[37],](#page-12-0) [[49],](#page-12-0) [[50].](#page-12-0) Therefore, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H4:* Facilitating conditions have a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *E. Hedonic Motivation*
Hedonic motivation denotes the degree to which an individual enjoys the usage of an information system [[34].](#page-12-0) Hedonic motivation has been considered a key element in various contexts, such as shopping, which explains why people intend to buy [[51].](#page-12-0) In the technology context, hedonic motivation refers to the joy experienced by individuals while interacting with information technology [[52],](#page-12-0) [[53].](#page-12-0) According to the literature, hedonic motivation was the second strongest factor influencing the students' acceptance of mobile learning in Malaysia [[54].](#page-12-0) The positive influence of hedonic motivation to adopt chatbots and other technological solutions for educational purposes is confirmed across several studies [[55],](#page-12-0) [[56].](#page-12-0) Thus, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H5:* Hedonic motivation has a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *F. Habit*
Habit signifies the extent to which individuals automatically behave due to their learning [[57].](#page-12-0) This perspective addresses whether students' habit will influence their use of chatbots to share knowledge. The significance of habits in influencing individuals' inclination to utilize different technological solutions has been proven by several studies [[58],](#page-12-0) [[59].](#page-12-0) In their study to investigate the determinants of using social networks, Abu Gharrah and Aljaafreh [[57]](#page-12-0) have confirmed the positive influence of habit on the actual use of social networks for academic purposes in Jordanian universities. Sugumar and Chandra [[38]](#page-12-0) also found that habit positively influences the adoption of chatbots for financial services. Therefore, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H6:* Habit has a significant positive effect on AI chatbot use.
## *G. Technology Threat Avoidance Theory*
TTAT explains the avoidance behavior that was disregarded by other preceding theories [[35],](#page-12-0) where the users' perceived threat of particular technology is controlled by the perceived severity and the perceived susceptibility to utilize that technology. The former can be defined as the insight of an individual about the degree of possible harm or negative results from using technology, while the latter can be described as the users' belief regarding the possibility of making bad decisions due to their usage of technology [[15],](#page-11-0) [[35],](#page-12-0) [[60].](#page-12-0)
Although research on information technology threats is still in its early stages, the TTAT has been employed in various settings to understand the factors that encourage users to avoid the threats of technology usage [[11],](#page-11-0) [[15],](#page-11-0) [[61],](#page-12-0) [[62],](#page-12-0) [[63].](#page-13-0) For instance, Cao et al. [[15]](#page-11-0) claimed that perceived severity and perceived susceptibility have a positive influence on the perceived threat, which was also confirmed by Carpenter et al. [[11].](#page-11-0) Accordingly, the following two hypotheses are proposed:
*H7:* Perceived severity has a significant positive effect on perceived threat.
*H8:* Perceived susceptibility has a significant positive effect on perceived threat.
The TTAT suggests that the perceived threat of technology negatively impacts technology adoption and avoids its use [[14],](#page-11-0) [[15],](#page-11-0) [[62],](#page-12-0) [[64].](#page-13-0) Warkentin et al. [[64]](#page-13-0) confirmed that information privacy and risk beliefs have a significant negative impact on the usage of smart metering technology. Breward et al. [[14]](#page-11-0) also investigated the adoption of biometric identity authentication in the banking sector and verified the significant negative impact of privacy and security concerns on the intention to use the proposed solution. Furthermore, the negative impact of perceived threats on using e-learning social media platforms by students [[62]](#page-12-0) and AI by managers [[15]](#page-11-0) have been hypothesized in the existing literature, but the empirical results were insignificant. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate this ongoing controversy regarding the significant influence of the expected threats on technology adoption and fulfill the gap accordingly. Consequently, the following hypothesis is proposed:
*H9:* Perceived threat has a significant negative effect on AI chatbot use.
# IV. RESEARCH METHODOLOGY
## *A. Data Collection and Research Instrument*
This research employs a quantitative survey methodology to measure the variables underpinning the proposed ICAAM. This method is appropriate in studies where validated scales measure the variables. The nonprobability convenience sampling technique is adopted in this study since it is affordable, effective, easy to use, and practical for collecting high-quality data. The COVID-19 pandemic lockdown made face-to-face interactions with respondents difficult, so an online survey using Google Forms was the most efficient way to collect the data. The questionnaire surveys were distributed among university students studying at two different universities in Malaysia. The participants confirmed that they are all actual users of chatbots. The consent was obtained electronically from the respondents by agreeing to participate in the study at the beginning of the survey. To avoid missing data issues, all the questions were made obligatory. One thousand students in total were invited to take part in the survey. A total of 447 respondents—representing a response rate of 44.7%—provided complete answers to the survey questions and were thus included in the research. Table [I](#page-5-0) shows the demographic profile of respondents.
A five-point Likert scale ranging from (1 = "strongly disagree") to (5 = "strongly agree") was used to measure the items of each construct. The items of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, and habit were adopted from [[34].](#page-12-0) The items of perceived severity were adopted from [[65].](#page-13-0) The items of perceived susceptibility and perceived threat were adopted from [[15],](#page-11-0) whereas the items of chatbot use were adopted from [[37].](#page-12-0)
## *B. Analytical Procedures*
The Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 25 was used for the descriptive analysis and common method bias (CMB). Second, the PLS-SEM technique via SmartPLS was used to examine the proposed relationships in ICAAM. The PLS-SEM technique evaluates the validity and reliability of constructs and indicators. This is achieved by assessing the outer measurement model as a preliminary step to evaluating the inner structural model. We have then assessed the configurational model of the study using the fsQCA [[66],[67],[68].](#page-13-0)Mechanisms that symmetrical techniques would have overlooked can be discovered using fsQCA [[17].](#page-11-0)

*1) Calibration:* In fsQCA, each determinant is represented as a fuzzy set with varying membership values [[66].](#page-13-0) The first phase of fsQCA is to calibrate all questionnaire data. In this situation, values extend from (5 = "strongly agree") to (1 = "strongly disagree") into fuzzy set meanings. There are two ways to calibrate: indirectly (by qualitatively examining the cases and rescaling the original measures) or directly (by ascertaining three distinctive positions of membership in a set: complete nonmembership, crossover, and complete membership) [[66],](#page-13-0) [[69].](#page-13-0) When dealing with experimental observations, such as the Likert scale, it is recommended to employ the direct calibration technique. This method requires figuring out the three scale membership points. The scale utilized in this study required the employment of a direct calibration technique with three anchors: responses with a membership score of 0 were categorized as full nonmembers, 1 served as the cutoff for full membership, and 0.5 served as the crossover point [[72].](#page-13-0) All possible values for the fuzzy set elements were converted using a nonlinear stepwise logistic function built into the fsQCA program after the appropriate thresholds for each component were established [[66],](#page-13-0) [[69].](#page-13-0)
*2) Sufficiency Analysis:* Investigating the connections between configurations, or combinations, of cause conditions (i.e., factors), and the outcome (i.e., dependent variable) is the second step of the fsQCA evaluation. Boolean algebra is used to construct a set of suitable circumstances, often known as configurations, causal models, or recipes [[69].](#page-13-0) The significance
of the data is then determined via sufficient analysis, also known as truth table evaluation, utilizing two parameters: consistency and coverage levels of 0.8 and 0.2, respectively. Coverage is comparable to the coefficient of determination (*R*2), which quantifies how much each causal explanation influences a result. From 0 to 1, there are several levels of coverage; a greater value denotes more thorough covering. Like the correlation coefficient (β), consistency evaluates how much a causative condition contributes to the observed outcome. [[66].](#page-13-0) Three solutions are generated when truth tables are analyzed using the fsQCA software: complex, intermediate, and parsimonious. We have used the intermediate solution, a subset of complicated solutions containing parsimonious answers [[69].](#page-13-0)
*3) Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA):* The last step in the fsQCA analysis is to figure out what conditions are needed. This is called NCA, which refers to the study of whether the unique effects of each antecedent condition are important for the outcome. The literature suggests that a condition exists when the result is virtually always obvious [[66],](#page-13-0) [[67].](#page-13-0) If the consistency scores of a necessary component are above 0.90, it can be confirmed that it is truly the case [[66],](#page-13-0) [[73].](#page-13-0)
# V. RESULTS
## *A. Nonresponse and Common Method Bias*
To examine the likelihood of nonresponse bias, Levene's homogeneity of variance test is used [[74].](#page-13-0) As per the one-way ANOVA results, nonresponse bias is not an issue for the study. There were no significant differences between early and late responders. In addition, CMB in self-report surveys can reduce the confirmability of notions and proposed associations within a theoretical framework [[75].](#page-13-0) We have reduced and quantified CMB prevalence using a mix of procedural and numerical treatments. ## *E. Analysis of Necessary Conditions*
NCA is performed to assess whether or not the individual effect of each antecedent condition is necessary for the set objective. A "necessary condition" is a type of causative circumstance that is still existing when the result is determined. The necessary component should have consistency ratings higher than 0.90 and coverage higher than 0.5 [[81],](#page-13-0) [[82].](#page-13-0) The evidence presented in Table [VI](#page-9-0) reveals that only EE is necessary for achieving a higher level of chatbot use for knowledge sharing. This observation suggests that if students' effort expectations, also known as ease of use, are not met, it will prevent them from achieving their objective of using chatbots for knowledge-sharing purposes.

This finding implies that students are more likely to use AI chatbots if they find them useful for knowledge sharing and easy to use. As such, developers should give special attention to the functionality and user-friendliness of AI chatbots. Furthermore, universities are required to offer students training on how to use AI chatbots and how they can enhance students' productivity and assist them in completing their tasks.
The association between social influence and AI chatbot use was not supported. This finding is not in line with prior studies [[47],](#page-12-0) [[48],](#page-12-0) which found social influence as a significant driver of intention to use chatbots. This result is quite surprising, as consumers in collectivist countries tend to conform to social norms. There are two possible explanations for this insignificant relationship. First, as chatbots are in their early stages of development, it will take time to become social norms. Previous studies have shown that social influence does not influence the adoption of new products which have not yet penetrated the mass market [[83].](#page-13-0) Second, students form the sample of the study. Educated people are less likely to be affected by social norms and tend to value systems according to their own experiences rather than being influenced by others [[84].](#page-13-0)
The influence of facilitating conditions on AI chatbot use was not supported, which is inconsistent with prior observations[[37],](#page-12-0) [[49].](#page-12-0) Facilitating conditions refer to having knowledge of how to use chatbots or being able to obtain support when needed.
One possible explanation for this insignificant relationship is that students know how to find educational resources if they encounter difficulties while using chatbots. For instance, they are familiar with how to use YouTube to understand chatbots. As such, the existence of support does not affect their decision to use chatbots. This finding may also be explained by being technologically savvy. Since students are highly familiar with the use of technology, the facilitating conditions are not a significant factor in their decision to use chatbots [[85].](#page-13-0)
The findings also showed an insignificant relationship between hedonic motivation and AI chatbot use. This result is not in agreement with the findings of previous research [[55].](#page-12-0) It means students do not use AI chatbots for having fun or entertainment. This result is logical considering the utilitarian value of using chatbots for knowledge sharing. Earlier findings have found that hedonic motivation has no impact on the use of utilitarian systems [[86].](#page-13-0) Students use chatbots to accomplish their tasks more efficiently and effectively rather than for entertainment and fun.
The study confirmed the influence of habit on AI chatbot use. This result is consistent with earlier research findings [[38],](#page-12-0) [[57].](#page-12-0) This further supports the argument that habit is a driver of behavior. Lecturers can provide hands-on demonstrations and encourage students to use chatbots in the classroom to create the habit of using them. Furthermore, when students ask questions that chatbots can answer, instructors may advise them to use chatbots to obtain the necessary information.
In line with the previous findings [[15],](#page-11-0) [[62],](#page-12-0) the symmetric results identified perceived threat as a negative driver of AI chatbot use. This implies that students may avoid using AI chatbots due to their privacy and security concerns. The study also found that perceived severity and susceptibility are major factors associated with a perceived threat. As such, universities should address students' concerns about vulnerability to security
and data protection incidents and getting wrong and inaccurate information. Furthermore, universities should develop regulations that support the security of knowledge sharing via chatbots. Universities should also offer instructions to students so they can learn more about chatbots and the kinds of inquiries they can ask them. Chatbot developers should also continuously improve the reliability and security of chatbots and address their errors. Chatbots should be able to connect students to help desks if they require additional information or are not certain that the provided information is accurate.
The fsQCA identified four combinations of factors that explain high chatbot usage (see solutions for high use in Table [V)](#page-8-0) and three combinations that explain low chatbot usage (see solutions for low use in Table [V)](#page-8-0). The overall coverage of fsQCA was 0.705, which is higher than the explanatory power of PLS (0.570). It is evident from these findings that one single solution does not provide the best explanation for students' use of chatbots. Students are heterogeneous and have different perceptions and needs, so different factors may motivate or discourage them from using chatbots. The importance of the factors depends on personal (e.g., technology savvy) and situational (e.g., stage of adoption) factors. Interestingly, in M2 and M3, students who use chatbots frequently report a high effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and performance expectancy, as well as low facilitating conditions, habits, and perceived threats. The results of model 4 are the opposite, and students who use chatbots heavily reported a high facilitating condition, habit, and perceived threat and low effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and performance expectancy. These findings imply that in the early stages of chatbot adoption, when chatbot usage is not a habit, students are more likely to use chatbots if they find using them to be enjoyable, easy to use, useful, free of risk, and supported by others. However, as the use of chatbots becomes habitual, it is essential to ensure that facilitating conditions are available.
Although, according to PLS-SEM results, the perceived threat was the most influential factor and should receive the highest attention, the fsQCA reveals that effort expectancy is the only necessary factor for AI chatbot use. This illustrates the complexity of human behaviors and their dependency on situational and personal characteristics. As such, a single model cannot provide a holistic view of AI chatbot use. Currently, the use of chatbots is in its infancy and has not yet become habitual among most students (Models 1–3). Effort expectancy is a necessary factor that should be given special consideration. Earlier studies argued that fsQCA provides a more robust illustration of individuals' behavior in comparison to PLS [[67],](#page-13-0) [[69].](#page-13-0) Our study illustrates the value of asymmetrical analysis and the dangers of relying solely on symmetrical analysis.
# VII. CONCLUSION
## *A. Theoretical Contributions*
The study extends the literature on AI chatbots in various ways. First, the study extends UTAUT2 by incorporating the TTAT factors. The findings confirmed that perceived threats negatively influence AI chatbot adoption. Besides beneficial
factors, such as performance expectancy and effort expectancy, risk factors (perceived threats) play an essential role in shaping the extent of chatbot use. The proposed model strengthens the explanatory power of UTAUT2 in the chatbot context. Second, unlike previous studies that investigated the determinants of chatbot use using a symmetric approach [[15],](#page-11-0) [[48],](#page-12-0) this study used an asymmetric approach (fsQCA) as a complementary analysis approach. The overall coverage of four combinations of factors for explaining chatbot use proposed by fsQCA is 0.705, which is higher than the explanatory power of PLS (0.570). This shows students' behaviors towards chatbots are complex, and the determinants of their behaviors are different. One best set of factors does not exist, and the influence of factors depends on situational and personal factors. Among 4 sets of factors that explain high chatbot use, M1-M3 showed the factors that influence chatbot use at the early stage of adoption, as the members of these three solutions reported a low level of habitual use of chatbots. However, M4 explains the behaviors of students that use chatbots habitually. As such, the adoption stage plays a vital role in the extent to which factor influences chatbot use and a single model cannot explain the drivers of chatbots in both the pre-adoption and post-adoption stages.
Although effort expectancy, social influence, and hedonic motivation are high among members of M1-M4, and facilitation conditions, habit, and perceived threat are low, the level of other factors (perceived severity, perceived susceptibility, and performance expectancy) are different among them. This demonstrates the heterogeneity in the needs of users. Therefore, other than the adoption stage, personal factors may affect the importance of determinants among students. As such, the results of the symmetric approach cannot provide a realistic picture of how factors influence AI chatbot usage. It is worthwhile to highlight that, although according to symmetric results, social influence, facilitating conditions, and hedonic motivation have no impact on AI chatbot use, the asymmetric approach reveals all factors may play a role in shaping AI chatbot and stage of adoption and students' heterogeneity should be considered. In contrast to the results of PLS that found perceived threat as the most influential determinant of chatbot use, the fsQCA results found only effort expectancy as a necessary factor for chatbot use.
## *B. Practical Implications*
Practically, the findings enable universities, instructors, and chatbot developers to make insightful decisions and successfully promote AI chatbots' use. A special focus should be given to ease of use to increase student-chatbot penetration. Chatbot developers should design a user-friendly chatbot. As many brands and government agencies provide chatbot services and many students have experience working with them, a chatbot for knowledge sharing should share a similar interface with other chatbots that students are familiar with to enhance userfriendliness and ease of use. Effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence, and hedonic motivation should all be intense in the early stages of chatbot adoption when use is not habitual. Accordingly, universities should provide training to demonstrate the functionality of chatbots and make
it possible for students to utilize chatbots more efficiently and effectively.
Considering the importance of social influence, instructors, as important influencers for students, should demonstrate their support for using chatbots for information sharing. Furthermore, universities may provide a platform where students share their experiences with chatbots and motivate others to use them. The study also found hedonic motivation as an important driver of using chatbots in the early stages. Therefore, chatbot trainers may introduce chatbots as an entertaining tool for sharing knowledge. The extent of perceived threat should also be low at the early stage of chatbot adoption. To motivate students to use chatbots, it is important to address their concerns regarding the risk of receiving incorrect information as well as security and data protection incidents.
Chatbot developers should continually improve the security and reliability of chatbots and resolve any errors that arise. Universities should develop policies and procedures to ensure the security of knowledge sharing using chatbots. Instructors should also assure students that chatbots are secure. Interestingly, the results showed that facilitating conditions play an important role in chatbot use in the post-adoption stage (high habit). Therefore, universities should establish a help desk where students can seek assistance if they encounter difficulties while working with chatbots.
## *C. Limitations and Future Work*
The study has some limitations, which offer suggestions for future research. First, the sample of the study was limited to students in Malaysia. Future studies can test the model of this study in other geographical locations to enhance the generalizability of the findings. Second, the findings of the asymmetric approach categorized the influential determinants of AI chatbot use into three groups (M1–M3) at the early stage of adoption (low habit). Although the extent of most factors (effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, facilitating conditions, and perceived treats) are similar among them, the importance of performance expectancy, perceived severity, and perceived susceptibility is different among them. Accordingly, future studies are recommended to include personality-related factors such as innovativeness, technology savvy, self-esteem, and self-efficacy to differentiate between these three types of students. Finally, the study assessed the determinants of AI chatbot use, drawing on UTAUT2 and TTAT. Future studies are recommended to investigate the influential factors from other theoretical lenses, such as protection motivation theory, diffusion of innovation, and task-technology fit.
